newsitem.title: USA: Second week of jury selection starts in tobacco case.
newsitem.headline: Second week of jury selection starts in tobacco case.

text.p: A woman whose husband and father died recently from smoking-related cancers and another who said she did not believe secondhand smoke causes disease were added to list of jurors passing initial muster Monday in a landmark $5 billion lawsuit against the tobacco industry.
Jury selection was sluggish at the beginning of the second week of trial in the closely watched class-action lawsuit, with just 19 candidates questioned and only five added to the pool.

The lawsuit, known as Broin vs. Philip Morris et al, seeks damages from nine tobacco companies and industry groups on behalf of some 60,000 flight attendants who say they were sickened by secondhand smoke on U.S.-based passenger jets.

After admitting 32 of the first 75 prospective jurors questioned last week, Dade County Judge Robert Kaye had hoped to speed the process, ruling Friday that the candidates should be questioned in groups of six.

But early Monday he decided to continue the questioning individually when lawyers expressed concern that prejudicial statements uttered by one candidate could taint all six and lead to their exclusion.

The admissions brought the pool of prospects to 37. Because each side will be able to exclude 27 without explanation, the pool must be at least 60 to seat a panel of six, plus additional candidates to serve as alternates.

Among those found acceptable was a truck driver who opposed the smoking ban on U.S. domestic airline flights; an unemployed restaurant worker who said her two-pack-a-day habit helped calm her nerves; and a woman who said she did not believe secondhand smoke caused cancer.
Kaye excused one potential juror who said he had strong opinions against cigarette smoking and thought it would be unfair to put him on the jury.

Another possible juror, a former firefighter, said he believed smoke had negative health effects and offered that tobacco companies would have to prove to him that secondhand smoke did not cause disease.
